timeline: A cold Friday, in the garden of the royal chancery. An old secretary has just carried the sultan's letters in and out, as he has done for nearly thirty years. He sits down, and suddenly his body will not obey him. His young assistant, who will one day write it all down, is not far away.

Welcome to The Honest Historian. I'm Mehdi Rahmani, and this is Folio Five. In the last four folios, you have heard about viziers, princes, generals and caliphs. Today our hero holds no sword and wears no crown. He holds a pen.

His name was Bu Nasr Moshkan. For nearly thirty years he wrote the letters of two sultans. He knew their secrets, he guarded their words, and he walked every day beside a throne that could kill him. And he was the teacher of the man who wrote our book.

First, the place where he worked. Every great court in medieval Iran had a set of offices, called divans. One handled money. One handled the army. And one handled letters. In Persian it was called the divan-e resalat, the office of correspondence. We might call it the royal chancery.

This was where the sultan's words became writing. Letters to the caliph in Baghdad. Letters to the khans of Central Asia. Orders to governors, treaties, warnings, secret reports. Every one of them had to be written in beautiful Persian or Arabic, sealed, and sent.
And every one of them, if it was wrong by a single word, could start a war or end a career.

From around the year one thousand and eleven, the head of this office at Ghazni was Bu Nasr Moshkan. His full name was Abu Nasr Mansur, son of Moshkan. He ran the chancery for Sultan Mahmud, the great conqueror, and then, after Mahmud died, for his son Masud, the sultan we met in Folios Two and Three.
Bu Nasr was a master of both languages. Beyhaqi praised his writing again and again, and copied some of his letters into the history, so that they would not be lost.
Around the year ten twenty, a young man from the district of Beyhaq, in Khorasan, came to work in this office. He was about twenty five years old. His name was Abolfazl. We know him as Beyhaqi.

Bu Nasr took him in as an assistant and a pupil. Beyhaqi would work at his side for nineteen years. He watched how his master wrote, how he spoke to kings, when he spoke, and above all when he stayed silent. Beyhaqi calls him, again and again, ustadam, which means my master, or my teacher.
And much of what Beyhaqi tells us about the court of Masud, he saw from his master's desk, or heard from his master's mouth.
So when we read Beyhaqi, we are often hearing two voices. The pupil writes. But the teacher is standing just behind him.

Soon after Masud took the throne, in the year ten thirty, the court was full of fear. The new sultan was bringing back an old vizier, Ahmad Hasan, and men who had served the old order wondered who would be next to fall. Beyhaqi tells us plainly that his master was very afraid.
For a time, Bu Nasr stopped coming to sit in the chancery at all.
Masud sent for him. He spoke kindly to him, praised him, and sent him back to work. Beyhaqi reports that the sultan said a man like Bu Nasr was worth ten men to them.

But at a court, praise draws enemies. A rival named Bu Sahl Zawzani, a clever and bitter man, went to the sultan with a suggestion. Bu Nasr was rich, he said. If the sultan pressed him, three hundred thousand dinars could be squeezed out of him for the treasury.
Masud listened to the offer. And then he answered. He refused. He would not ruin a servant like that.

Then the sultan tested his secretary in another way. He asked for his advice on great matters of state. And Bu Nasr hesitated. He said he would rather not give advice, because others at court would call it overreaching, a secretary playing at being a minister. Only when Masud insisted on a frank answer did he speak.

His advice was simple. Follow the path of your late father, Mahmud, and do not speak ill of it. And keep the two armies united. By this he meant the old soldiers of Mahmud and the new men who had come up with Masud. If those two groups turned against each other, he warned, the kingdom would split.
It was good advice. As we will see, it was not always followed.
Now, do you remember Folio One, and Hasanak, the vizier on the gallows? Bu Nasr was at court on that terrible day, in the year ten thirty two.

Beyhaqi gives us one small detail about his master that I have never forgotten. He says that on the day of the hanging, Bu Nasr did not break his fast. He would not eat. He was deeply troubled, and he kept saying one thing.
Che omid manad?
What hope is left?

Think about what that means. Bu Nasr could not stop the hanging. Nobody could. If he had protested in public, he might have followed Hasanak to the gallows. So he did the only thing a careful man could do. He refused to eat, and he grieved where his pupil could see. And his pupil wrote it down.

Now we jump forward to the year ten thirty nine. The empire was in trouble. Nomad Turkmen horsemen, led by the Seljuq family, had come out of the steppe and were raiding Khorasan, the rich eastern province of Iran. Masud's army, huge and heavy, kept chasing them and kept losing.
The summer was hot, the fodder ran out, and the horses grew weak.
One night, with the news getting worse and worse, Masud sent for Bu Nasr, alone. Not the vizier, not the generals. The secretary. And he asked him what he really thought.

This was the most dangerous question a courtier could be asked. Tell a proud king the truth, and you may lose his favor. Flatter him, and you may lose the kingdom. Bu Nasr was quiet for a moment. And then, carefully, he told the sultan what he thought.
He said that these defeats looked to him like a sign that God was displeased. He urged the sultan to pray, to repent, and to make a vow that very night. And he used an old Persian saying.
Dowlat o mellat do baradar-and.
The state and the faith are two brothers. In other words, a ruler cannot be strong for long if he forgets what is right.
Then he turned practical. An army dragging so much baggage, he said, cannot fight the fast riders of the steppe. Separate the fighting men from the heavy loads.

Beyhaqi tells us that Masud accepted, and said that he would do it. But later, Bu Nasr spoke to his pupil in private, and he was close to despair. He said he wished they had died, rather than live to see such disgrace.
In the autumn of that same year, around the festival of Mehregan, Bu Nasr was wounded in a different way. Not by an enemy army, but by his rivals at court.

A list was drawn up of officials who would have to supply horses and camels for the war. Beyhaqi tells us that Bu Nasr's name was put on it, and he believed it was done on purpose, to provoke him, because everyone knew he would not keep quiet.

He did not keep quiet. He sent the sultan a sharp message. In Beyhaqi's words, prison, disgrace, poverty and even death had become sweet to him, compared with this humiliation. Coming from the most careful man at court, those words must have shocked everyone.

Masud was angry, but not with Bu Nasr. Beyhaqi reports that he said the fault was not his secretary's, and he made peace with him, and honored him again at his table. For a while, it seemed the storm had passed.
It had not. Not long after, on a very cold day, Bu Nasr carried letters in to the sultan and back out again, as he had done for nearly thirty years. Then, in the garden by the chancery, he collapsed.
Beyhaqi describes it as a stroke, coming in waves, one after another, within an hour. His face twisted, and his body would not obey him. A physician was brought. He said there was nothing to be done.

When the news reached Masud, Beyhaqi tells us, the sultan cried out, Alas for Bu Nasr. Great men of the court wept. Bu Nasr was carried home, and soon after, he died. It was the year ten thirty nine, or in the Islamic calendar, four hundred and thirty one.

Now here, Beyhaqi does something that shows us exactly why we can trust him. He reports a rumor. Some people said that the day before, at a garden party, Bu Nasr had been given drinks that did him harm. A lesser writer would have turned this into a murder story. Beyhaqi does not.
He tells us what people said, and then he says, in effect, that he will not judge. He leaves it there.
That is the honest historian at work. He loved this man. He had every reason to blame someone. And still he would not write more than he knew.

What did Bu Nasr leave behind? Beyhaqi tells us that before he died, his master had asked the sultan to look after him, his pupil. And when the chancery needed a new head, Masud said privately that if Beyhaqi had not been so young, the post would have been his. He was about forty six.
At that court, apparently, that was still young.
Instead, the job went to Bu Sahl Zawzani, the same rival who had once offered to squeeze the old man for three hundred thousand dinars. Beyhaqi became his deputy. You can imagine how that felt.

And Beyhaqi wrote his master an epitaph in Arabic, which means, roughly, that with him, ability, eloquence and good sense came to an end. He also says something sadder. For thirty years, he writes, his master did not have a single truly happy day.
A man at the very top of the government, trusted by two sultans, honored, rich. And not one happy day. That is the price of standing so close to the throne.

So, how does a secretary survive at a dangerous court? Bu Nasr's answer seems to be: speak rarely, speak carefully, and when you finally speak, tell the truth. And when you cannot change what is happening, at least do not pretend it is right.
If there is one lesson here, it is this: you may not be able to stop an injustice, but you can refuse to call it justice.
Next week, we go hunting with Sultan Masud, and meet a lion. It is one of the most famous scenes in Beyhaqi, and it tells us a great deal about the kind of man Masud really was.

If you enjoyed this story, follow the show so you don't miss the next one, and share it with someone who loves history. I'm Mehdi Rahmani. This episode was retold from the Persian original of the History of Beyhaqi, and narrated with an AI rendering of my own voice. Thank you for listening.
